questions.question: What is the defining constraint of a one-time signature (OTS) scheme?
options: A keypair must sign at most one message
A public key can verify at most one signature
A signature must be exactly one hash long
Verification requires no public key
questions.explanation: OTS security only holds if each keypair is used to sign at most one message; reusing the key can leak enough material to enable forgeries.

questions.question: In a Merkle tree, what does an authentication path typically contain?
options: The private keys for every leaf
The list of sibling hashes from the leaf level up to the root
A random nonce used to salt every internal node
A full copy of the entire tree
questions.explanation: An auth path is the minimal set of sibling hashes needed to recompute the root from a given leaf.

questions.question: In a basic Merkle signature scheme (MSS), what is the long-term public key most verifiers pin to?
options: A Merkle root (plus pinned parameters like hash and tree height)
A single Lamport secret key
The concatenation of all leaf private keys
The last signature produced by the signer
questions.explanation: The Merkle root commits to all leaf public keys; verification also requires the verifier to know the parameters used to build that root.

questions.question: Why must a Merkle signature include the leaf index (or equivalent position information)?
options: So the verifier can choose the correct sibling order while hashing up the path
So the verifier can recover the signer's master secret
So the verifier can compress the signature to a single byte
So the verifier can skip checking the authentication path
questions.explanation: At each level the verifier must know whether the current hash is a left or right child; the index determines the ordering with each sibling.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what is the most common catastrophic failure in stateful Merkle-tree signature schemes like XMSS/LMS?
options: Reusing the same leaf/OTS key index due to crashes, rollbacks, or concurrency bugs
Using SHA-256 instead of SHA-512
Including the auth path in the signature
Storing the public root in a certificate
questions.explanation: Leaf reuse breaks the 'one-time' assumption of the OTS layer and can leak enough material to enable forgeries.

questions.question: What must an MSS verifier check to accept a signature?
options: Only that the authentication path recomputes the public root
Only that the OTS signature verifies under the included leaf public key
Both OTS verification and Merkle membership (auth path) to the pinned root
Neither; MSS signatures are self-authenticating
questions.explanation: MSS has two layers: the OTS signature must verify, and the leaf public key must be proven to be part of the committed set via the auth path.

questions.question: What does domain separation mean in this context, and why does it matter?
options: Using different hash functions for leaves and internal nodes to speed up verification
Prefixing/labeling hashes for different purposes to prevent cross-protocol or cross-layer collisions
Encrypting the Merkle root so attackers cannot see it
Changing the tree height for every signature
questions.explanation: Domain separation uses labels/prefixes so that a hash intended as a leaf cannot be interpreted as an internal node (or vice versa) in another context.

questions.question: How do stateful schemes (XMSS/LMS) differ from stateless schemes (SPHINCS+) operationally?
options: Stateful schemes require leaf index management; stateless schemes avoid it but typically have larger signatures
Stateful schemes are always faster and smaller than stateless schemes in every parameter set
Stateless schemes require keeping a counter on disk; stateful schemes do not
They are operationally identical; only the names differ
questions.explanation: Stateful schemes must ensure indices never repeat (which is operationally hard); stateless schemes avoid that requirement at the cost of different performance/size trade-offs.
